title: Best Hiking Boots UK
short: Walking and hiking boots compared by grip, waterproofing and support, from budget trail boots to technical mountain footwear.
intro: The right hiking boot balances weight against support and waterproofing, and that balance shifts depending on the terrain and how much you're carrying. This guide compares boots tested by Live for the Outdoors' team of hiking experts on thousands of miles of UK and mountain terrain.

products.name: Aequilibrium Hike GTX
products.best_for: Rugged hillwalking, scrambling and mixed technical terrain
products.key_spec: Vibram outsole, 3D Flex System Evo, Gore-Tex, 535g per boot
products.summary: LFTO's best in test, feeling planted and precise the moment terrain gets steep and rocky, with a Vibram outsole that grips hard on wet rock and a pronounced heel brake for confidence on descents. A tough synthetic upper is comfortable out of the box, though it's firmly premium-priced and slightly heavy for big-mileage days.
pros: Proven design suited to rugged mountain use
Reliable waterproofing in wet grass and soggy trails
cons: Less comfortable than ultralight boots on big mileage days
products.search: La Sportiva Aequilibrium Hike GTX boots

products.name: Rush Trk Pro GTX
products.best_for: Buyers who want a lightweight yet protective three-season boot
products.key_spec: Oiled nubuck leather, Presa Supergum outsole, chunky EVA midsole
products.summary: Won LFTO's Trail Gear of the Year, with generous ankle padding via a 3D Autofit collar and excellent traction from Scarpa's own outsole. Metal lacing hardware adds durability, giving a sturdy, protective boot that still feels light and agile, though it only comes in one width so the fit won't suit everyone.
pros: Impressive performance for a relatively lightweight boot
cons: Single width won't suit everyone's foot shape
products.search: Scarpa Rush Trk Pro GTX boots

products.name: MH500 Mountain
products.best_for: Casual hikers who want comfort on woodland and dry hill trails
products.key_spec: 395g per boot, no break-in period, basic waterproofing
products.summary: A genuine surprise at under £75, feeling more like a sturdy trainer than a traditional boot, with no stiffness or break-in period and decent underfoot cushioning. LFTO found grip better than expected on typical countryside terrain, though waterproofing lets water in during sustained rain or boggy ground.
pros: Lightweight and comfortable from the first wear
cons: Waterproofing struggles in heavy rain or boggy terrain

products.name: Tibet Evo GTX
products.best_for: Multi-day treks or carrying a heavy pack over rough terrain
products.key_spec: 768g per boot, Vibram Apptrail Divo outsole, dual-zone lacing
products.summary: A full-fat trekking boot that LFTO found brings a level of stability lighter designs can't match, with a stiff DuraPU midsole giving controlled foot placement on uneven ground. Grip and waterproofing both proved rock solid, and despite the stiffness, comfort surprised testers with little break-in needed.
cons: Too heavy and stiff for casual hikers

products.name: Aenergy Mtn Mid GTX
products.best_for: Big-mileage three-season hiking where comfort matters most
products.key_spec: Thick EVA midsole, Vibram Megagrip outsole, jacquard mesh upper
products.summary: Became a boot LFTO's testers kept reaching for without thinking, thanks to a soft, bouncy EVA midsole with noticeable energy return that takes the sting out of long descents. Grip and waterproofing were both dependable on mixed UK terrain, though it's not built for the toughest mountain days or wintry conditions.
pros: Great midsole cushioning with energy return
cons: Not built for the toughest terrain or harshest weather
products.search: Mammut Aenergy Mtn Mid GTX boots

products.name: Aequilibrium LT GTX
products.best_for: Mixed winter mountain terrain, including crampon use
products.key_spec: PU foam injected sole, semi-automatic C2 crampon compatible, nubuck leather upper
products.summary: LFTO calls this the ideal mountain boot for balancing walking comfort, technical performance and durability, with an unusual PU-foam-injected sole that saves weight without losing cushioning. A flexible, elasticated ankle cuff gave excellent freedom of movement, though the narrower last won't suit every foot.
cons: Less precise crampon fit than dedicated winter boots
products.search: La Sportiva Aequilibrium LT GTX boots

products.name: Innovo Mid GTX
products.best_for: Buyers who want a firm, supportive all-rounder for most UK conditions
products.key_spec: Higher collar, 3 lace eyelets, Gore-Tex, Lowa rubber outsole
products.summary: Sits in a non-specialised middle ground between trainer-style boots and heavier leather options, with a higher collar and extra lace eyelet for a properly locked-in fit. LFTO found the firm, stable underfoot feel suits mountainous terrain well, with reliable grip and waterproofing, though it's too firm for those who prefer plush cushioning.
pros: Very good grip on gravel, rock and mud
cons: Too firm underfoot for some hikers

products.name: Targhee IV Waterproof Hiking Boot
products.best_for: Hikers who need a genuinely wide toe box
products.key_spec: KEEN.FUSION bonded sole, KEEN.RUGGED outsole, Luftcell midsole
products.summary: Keen's most popular model, known for its wide fit, now built more durably by fusing the sole to the upper with heat and pressure instead of glue. LFTO found it a capable three-season hillwalking boot with a more compression-resistant midsole than typical EVA foam, though grip on muddy terrain isn't the best on test.
cons: Not the best grip on muddy terrain

guide.q: Do I need a full leather boot or a lightweight fabric one?
guide.a: A full leather boot, like the Lowa Tibet Evo here, gives the most support and durability for multi-day treks or carrying a heavy pack, at the cost of extra weight. A lightweight fabric boot, like the Mammut or Quechua here, suits day walks and easier terrain where comfort and low weight matter more than maximum support.

guide.q: How waterproof do I actually need my boots to be?
guide.a: For typical UK countryside walking in wet grass and light rain, most Gore-Tex or similar membrane boots cope fine. For boggy, saturated ground or sustained heavy rain, prioritise a boot specifically praised for this, like the Lowa Tibet Evo or Innovo here, since budget waterproofing can let water in over time.

guide.q: Do I need a specific winter or crampon-compatible boot?
guide.a: If you're hiking on snow or ice and may need crampons, look for a boot rated for semi-automatic (C2) crampon compatibility, like the La Sportiva Aequilibrium LT here. For three-season UK hillwalking without technical winter routes, a standard hiking boot is sufficient.

guide.q: How much does fit and last shape matter?
guide.a: A lot, since boots that don't match your foot shape can cause blisters or discomfort no matter how well-reviewed they are. Brands like Keen are known for wider fits, while others like Scarpa run narrower and only come in one width, so trying boots on, or checking a brand's typical fit, is worth doing before buying.
